entry.title: DisasterAgent: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Verifiable Disaster Report Generation From Remote Sensing Imagery
entry.summary: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.

entry.title: Toward Self-Evolving Geospatial Algorithms: An LLM-Driven Framework with a Case Study on Spatial Regime Discovery
entry.summary: Geospatial algorithms have been developed through expert-driven discovery: a researcher spots a limitation, proposes a structural fix, and checks it by hand. With LLM-driven multi-agent systems becoming practical, much of the candidate-generation, evaluation, and selection work can now be largely automated, while the researcher's role shifts upstream toward problem formulation, evaluation design, and interpretation. We refer to this paradigm as Self-Evolving Geospatial Algorithms (SEGA) and propose a framework with three required modules: a two-loop architecture with embedded geographic knowledge as the inner-loop engine; an automatic code formatter that converts any raw geospatial algorithm into the standardized triple required by the inner loop; and a simulation-driven training protocol, in which evolution runs only on synthetic data with known ground truth, and the discovered algorithm is applied unchanged to real data, keeping real-world results out-of-sample. We use spatial regime discovery as a case study, seeded with the Two-stage K-Models algorithm. Evolution uses the Rand Index against the ground-truth partition as fitness signal; the frozen algorithm is then evaluated on 150 simulated grids and 11 real-world datasets across climate, health, hydrology, and politics. The evolved algorithm outperforms its seed, knowledge-free baselines, and four classical regionalization methods. Ablations further indicate that the channel of geographic-knowledge injection, structured retrieval versus prompt-level hints, is itself load-bearing. In this case study, LLM-assisted search sped up the inner loop; whether it does so for other seeds and task families remains open. The geographer's role -- asking the right questions, designing trustworthy evaluation -- grows more central.

entry.title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
entry.summary: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.
